review_scope: U.S. prednisone immediate-release tablets and current selected generic delayed-release tablets, supplemented by historical FDA Rayos presentation, public 2024 adrenal-withdrawal recommendations and primary UK systemic-sclerosis safety warning.

paragraphs: Selected immediate-release labeling covers endocrine conditions, rheumatic/connective-tissue disease, severe allergic/skin/ocular inflammatory disorders, selected pulmonary/hematologic disorders, neoplastic palliation, nephrotic syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease. Examples include RA/lupus flares, severe asthma/allergy unresponsive to usual treatment, and ulcerative colitis/Crohn-type regional enteritis. Selected infections require appropriate anti-infective co-treatment. Hydrocortisone/cortisone are preferred for adrenal replacement; mineralocorticoids may also be needed.

Delayed-release labeling also includes selected transplant-rejection and additional disease indications. Treat its indication list as regulatory wording rather than a recommendation to use steroids for every listed condition. Choice, duration and combination treatment depend on contemporary disease guidance; this profile does not supply disease-specific flare protocols. Delayed release is not an emergency rescue substitute.

Both selected full labels describe initial doses often 5–60 mg/day; less severe illness may need less, and some conditions require more. Continue/adjust until response, then reduce to the lowest effective maintenance dose. Pediatric dosing follows disease severity and response rather than a single age/weight ratio. No universal pediatric mg/kg regimen or maximum is inferred.

rows: Immediate-release tablet
Take with food or milk to reduce stomach irritation. For a prescribed single daily dose, selected label favors morning before 9 am; divided schedules depend on the regimen.
Delayed-release prednisone / Rayos
Take with food; swallow intact, without breaking/dividing/chewing. Release starts ~4 hours after intake; choose timing for the disease and formulation. Do not automatically apply IR morning timing.
IR → delayed release

Prescriber uses an equivalent glucocorticoid dose based on relative potency and adapts timing; prednisone/prednisolone 5 mg correspond to methylprednisolone 4 mg or hydrocortisone 20 mg for the label’s oral/IV comparison.

paragraphs: The 2024 ESE/Endocrine Society guideline generally suggests no adrenal taper/testing for courses <3–4 weeks. Longer treatment should be tapered only when the disease is controlled and steroids are no longer needed; reduce toward physiologic prednisone-equivalent 4–6 mg/day, then individualize clinical monitoring or morning cortisol testing. Disease relapse and withdrawal symptoms may alter the plan. Labels caution against abrupt withdrawal after prolonged therapy; no fixed taper fits everyone.

No fixed eGFR/hepatic dose formula is provided. Renal insufficiency, hypertension and HF increase concerns from salt/water retention and potassium loss. Cirrhosis can enhance corticosteroid effects through reduced metabolism; thyroid status also affects clearance. Acute stress may require a rapidly acting steroid or supplemental coverage rather than relying on delayed-release timing.

items: Can cause HPA suppression, Cushing features and hyperglycemia; adrenal insufficiency may persist after withdrawal. Severe weakness, hypotension or vomiting after reduction/illness needs urgent assessment.

Infections may worsen, reactivate or be masked. Screen for hepatitis B before immunosuppressive/prolonged therapy; assess TB, Strongyloides or amebiasis risks as relevant. Varicella/measles exposure in a nonimmune patient needs prompt prophylaxis review.
Avoid systemic fungal infection except when required for a specific drug reaction under specialist care. Avoid live vaccines at immunosuppressive doses; inactivated responses may be reduced.
Monitor BP/fluid retention and potassium, especially with HF/renal disease; use great caution after recent MI. GI ulceration/perforation can occur with muted signs.

Mood changes, insomnia, mania, severe depression or psychosis, osteoporosis/fractures, myopathy, impaired healing and reduced child growth may occur. Cataracts/glaucoma and ocular infection require attention; avoid active ocular herpes simplex.

Systemic sclerosis requires particular caution: supplemental primary prednisolone labeling warns of potentially fatal scleroderma renal crisis. Monitor BP/creatinine; sudden hypertension or reduced urine needs urgent specialist assessment.

paragraphs: The selected immediate-release label formally contraindicates systemic fungal infection and ingredient hypersensitivity. The selected delayed-release section 4 lists hypersensitivity; fungal infection is an avoidance warning in section 5.2. Live vaccines are contraindicated at immunosuppressive corticosteroid doses. Distinguish the exact product’s section-4 wording from precautions.
No boxed warning appears in the selected prednisone tablet labels. Lack of a box does not reduce the significance of adrenal crisis, infection, bone loss or other systemic risks.

Reported effects include appetite/weight gain, edema, increased BP/glucose, insomnia/mood changes, dyspepsia, acne/bruising and poor wound healing. Prolonged therapy can cause adrenal suppression, osteoporosis/osteonecrosis, cataracts/glaucoma and serious infections. Rates vary with dose/duration and cannot be inferred from spontaneous reports. Suspected overdose needs prompt medical/toxicology guidance; do not induce vomiting at home or abruptly stop chronic treatment to correct excess exposure.

rows: CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, ritonavir, macrolides) / inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine)
Exposure can rise/fall; review response, systemic toxicity and adjustment.
NSAIDs / aspirin
GI adverse risk rises; aspirin clearance can change and withdrawal may increase salicylate levels.
Warfarin
Anticoagulant response may increase or decrease; monitor INR/coagulation more frequently.
Antidiabetic agents
Steroid glucose elevation may require treatment adjustment and more checks.
Potassium-depleting diuretics / amphotericin B; digoxin
Monitor potassium; hypokalemia increases arrhythmia risk with digoxin.
Cyclosporine
Both drugs’ effects may rise; seizures have been reported.
Anticholinesterases in myasthenia gravis
Severe weakness risk; specialist supervision and respiratory-support planning.
Fluoroquinolones
Tendon rupture risk increases, especially in older adults.
Bupropion / thalidomide
Review seizure risk / serious skin reaction risk respectively.
Vaccines / skin testing
Avoid live vaccine at immunosuppressive doses; immune/test responses may be blunted.

paragraphs: Human corticosteroid pregnancy studies show a small, inconsistent orofacial-cleft association; underlying disease can confound growth/birth-weight outcomes. Weigh maternal benefit and fetal risk and observe infants after substantial maternal doses for adrenal suppression. Prednisolone enters milk; modern delayed-release labeling estimates infant exposure <1% of maternal daily dose with no reported infant adverse effects in cited reports, but prolonged high doses may affect growth/adrenal function. Balance breastfeeding and maternal treatment individually.

Pediatric evidence includes nephrotic syndrome >2 years and aggressive leukemia/lymphoma >1 month, with other indications supported partly by adult evidence; these are evidence descriptions, not a universal minimum age. Individualize treatment and monitor height/growth, BP, weight and infection. Older adults need cautious dosing and surveillance for bone loss, diabetes, hypertension, edema and infection.

Selected delayed-release PK studies have not evaluated renal/hepatic impairment. IR labeling notes increased effects in cirrhosis and cautions in renal insufficiency/HF. Individualize and monitor metabolic/fluid effects rather than assuming a numeric adjustment or absence of risk.

Systemic glucocorticoid activity suppresses inflammatory/immune responses and affects glucose/protein/fat metabolism. Some mineralocorticoid activity contributes to sodium retention, hypertension and potassium loss; suppression of endogenous corticotropin contributes to adrenal suppression.

facts: Prednisone converts to active prednisolone; further metabolism occurs mainly in liver.
Approximately 4-hour lag; fed peak ~6–6.5 hours versus ~2 hours for IR in the cited comparison. Fasting decreases delayed-release exposure.
Prednisolone metabolites are excreted in urine as sulfate/glucuronide conjugates; terminal prednisone/prednisolone half-lives ~2–3 hours in the label comparison.
Equivalent total exposure with food does not make administration timing interchangeable.

items: Follow disease response and ongoing need; monitor BP, weight/edema, glucose and potassium during prolonged therapy.
Assess infection/exposure risk; obtain hepatitis B screening before immunosuppressive treatment and assess relevant latent infection risks.
Assess bone/fracture risk and preventive treatment; monitor children’s growth. Evaluate vision and check intraocular pressure with prolonged treatment (label threshold >6 weeks).
Monitor mood/sleep, GI bleeding or perforation symptoms, muscle weakness and signs of adrenal insufficiency during dose changes.
Follow the exact formulation schedule; take with food and swallow delayed-release tablets intact. Do not change a prolonged regimen without review.

Tell clinicians about current/recent steroid exposure before illness or surgery. If adrenal recovery is unconfirmed, stress coverage may be needed; hemodynamic instability or persistent vomiting requires urgent evaluation and parenteral treatment.
Report fever/infection exposure, black stools, severe mood changes, visual problems or profound weakness. Discuss vaccines before receiving them.
Keep an updated medicine list and a clinician-directed plan for tapering and missed doses.

paragraphs: Selected Par IR tablets: 1, 2.5, 5, 10 and 20 mg. Selected Dr. Reddy’s delayed-release label: 1 and 2 mg unscored tablets. The FDA Rayos brand label describes 1, 2 and 5 mg delayed-release tablets; this historical label does not establish current brand availability. Other tablet/liquid products require their own concentration and handling directions.

Selected IR tablets: 20–25°C in a tight light-resistant container. Selected delayed-release tablets: 20–25°C, excursions 15–30°C, protected from light/moisture in a tight light-resistant container. Keep out of children’s reach and preserve labeled release formulation identification.

scope_exclusions: No disease-specific flare regimen or universal taper is supplied; specialist protocols and current disease guidelines remain necessary.
Liquid products/concentrates and other manufacturers are not generalized from tablet labeling.
Rayos FDA label is explicitly historical; current marketed availability not asserted.
Supplemental prednisolone SmPC informs the systemic corticosteroid class safety warning only, not U.S. prednisone approvals.

resolved_source_findings.detail: IR formally lists systemic fungal infection as contraindicated; current selected DR section 4 lists hypersensitivity and places fungal infection in avoidance warning 5.2. Product-specific wording preserved.

Rayos highlights show initial 5 mg/day while full 2.1 and current generic DR label describe individualized 5–60 mg/day with higher doses possible. Full-section range is contextualized and never treated as a universal prescription.

Generic IR label includes older pregnancy category C and broad historical indication/bone-prophylaxis language. Profile uses modern DR pregnancy wording and does not propagate a universal label-only disease recommendation or older osteoporosis treatment threshold.

clinical_review: Every published card reviewed against full relevant primary label sections. Source-reviewed within stated scope; not an independent clinician sign-off.
blueprint: Immutable APAP eight sections, essential safety, three hero facts, cited disclosures, four safety cards and three product cards.
